## NATURAL-LANGUAGE HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded)

**Higher time preference (impatience) is associated with higher BMI.** In the NLSY79 sample, respondents who behaved more impatiently in 1989 — taking money out of savings or reporting no savings, versus putting money into savings — had a BMI about **0.7 BMI-units higher** at the 1992 survey (adjusted for demographics, family background, education, ability, and family income; p≈0.001). Each one-step increase on the savings-impatience scale (1 = put more in, 2 = took more out, 3 = no change, 4 = no savings) was associated with **+0.20 BMI units (95% CI ≈ +0.07 to +0.32; robust SE; p≈0.002)**, a standardized effect of ≈0.045 SD of BMI — roughly 0.6 kg for a 1.7-m adult. The direction is consistent across two independent patience proxies measured before/around the outcome: lower 1990 family net wealth (top wealth quintile ≈ **−0.92 BMI units** vs bottom quintile, p≈0.0002) and lower 1981 ASVAB Arithmetic Reasoning (**−0.24 BMI per 1-SD**, p≈0.002) each predict higher 1992 BMI after the same adjustment. The raw association is attenuated by roughly half once demographics/background/ability/income are controlled, and it appears for attained BMI in 1989 and 1992 but **not** for 1989→1992 weight gain (p≈0.88), indicating an association with the level of BMI rather than near-term weight change. Because the proxies are behavioral/wealth-based rather than a direct discounting measure, this is an **associational, temporally-ordered finding consistent with — but not proof that — increased time preference leads to higher BMI**; reverse causality (health/BMI affecting earnings, savings, and wealth) remains possible.

payload.hypothesis: Higher time preference (impatience), as proxied by 1989 savings behavior, is associated with higher BMI by 1992: each one-step increase on the savings-impatience scale is associated with about +0.20 BMI units (approx. 0.04-0.05 SD, approx. 0.6 kg for a 1.7 m adult) after adjusting for demographics, family background, education, ability, and family income (p ~ 0.002); corroborated by lower 1990 net wealth (top vs bottom quintile -0.9 BMI units) and lower 1981 ASVAB-AR (-0.24 BMI per SD) in the same direction. The association is attenuated by about half after controls, holds for attained BMI (1989 and 1992) but not for 1989->1992 weight gain, and is an associational, temporally-ordered pattern consistent with - but not proof that - increased time preference leads to higher BMI.
payload.workflow: Loaded NLSY79 (12,686 x 61). Derived BMI(1989/1992, change) from weight(lb->kg) and height(1985,in). Proxies: 1989 savings direction (primary; linear trend + dummy-coded), 1990 family net wealth (continuous z + quintiles), ASVAB-AR 1981 (z + terciles). OLS with HC1 robust SEs, unadjusted vs core vs extended confounder sets, complete-case with per-model n. Alt outcomes BMI1989 and BMI change 89->92; criminal proxies exploratory. Consolidated results in /workspace/model_summary.csv; main script /workspace/analysis_bmi_timepref.py.
